name: Types of Sleep Deprivation
what: This subtopic defines sleep deprivation and distinguishes between partial and full sleep deprivation based on the quantity and quality of sleep obtained within a 24-hour period. It establishes the foundational definitions needed to analyse the effects of insufficient sleep.
why: Precise definitions of partial versus full sleep deprivation are tested directly in VCE exams, and correctly applying these terms is essential for answering scenario-based questions about how much sleep a person has missed.

items.title: I can define sleep deprivation in terms of both quantity and quality of sleep
items.what: Sleep deprivation occurs when an individual does not obtain adequate sleep, either in terms of the total amount of sleep (quantity) or how restorative that sleep is (quality). It does not require a full 24 hours without sleep.
items.why: Students often incorrectly assume sleep deprivation only means no sleep at all. Understanding that poor-quality sleep also constitutes deprivation is necessary for applying the concept to realistic scenarios.
items.example: A student who sleeps for 8 hours but wakes frequently throughout the night and spends very little time in REM sleep may still be sleep deprived due to poor sleep quality, even though their total hours appear adequate.

items.title: I can define and distinguish partial sleep deprivation from full sleep deprivation
items.what: Partial sleep deprivation occurs when an individual receives some sleep within a 24-hour period but not an adequate quantity or quality. Full sleep deprivation occurs when an individual does not sleep at all for a period of 24 hours or more.
items.why: These two categories produce different levels of functional impairment and correspond to different BAC equivalents in the Dawson and Reid (1997) research, so distinguishing them is essential for exam questions.
items.example: If Ahmed stays up until 2am and wakes at 6am, getting only 4 hours of sleep, he is experiencing partial sleep deprivation. If Solomon does not sleep at all for 24 hours while studying, he is experiencing full sleep deprivation.

items.title: I can identify examples of partial sleep deprivation in everyday scenarios
items.what: Partial sleep deprivation arises in common situations such as staying up late, waking early, experiencing disrupted sleep due to noise, illness, anxiety, or caring for others. The person obtains some sleep but less than the recommended amount for their age group.
items.why: VCE questions frequently present real-world scenarios and ask students to correctly classify the type of sleep deprivation, so recognising partial deprivation in context is a regularly assessed skill.
items.example: A Year 12 student who normally needs 9 hours of sleep but only gets 5 hours the night before an exam because of anxiety is experiencing partial sleep deprivation, not full sleep deprivation.
